# Introduction

Welcome to your first workshop assignment for the Research Statistics with R (RSR) Bootcamp! In this week's exercise, you will use your understanding of the {tidyverse} package and RMarkdown to create a short report.

The goal of today's workshop is to reinforce your skills in **data wrangling**, **visualization**, and **reporting** using R.

**NOTE**: This course assumes knowledge of our Beginner R course content. Please refer to our textbook to look up any functions needed for this assignment: [datawithr.com](https://datawithr.com/){.uri}.

All assignments should be submitted individually, but you are encouraged to work in groups. To submit your work, please upload your assignment Rmd file to the Workshop 1 submission page.

# Instructions

Below, you'll find a series of tasks that guide you through importing, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset of COVID-19 patient records from two New York City hospitals. You can find the dataset CSV file and information about the dataset in the "data" subfolder.

These tasks should be completed in the `rsr_week_01_assignment.Rmd` file found in the "rmd" subfolder. We encourage you to have both this instructions document and the assignment document open.

## TASK 1: LOAD THE REQUIRED PACKAGES

Use `pacman::p_load()` to load the following packages: `{tidyverse}`, `{here}`, `{janitor}` and `{reactable}`.

Install the `{inspectdf}` package using the following code:

```{r}
pacman::p_load_current_gh("the-graph-courses/inspectdf")
```

## TASK 2: IMPORT THE DATA & INSPECT VARIABLES

Use `read_csv()` and `here()` to import the "covid_19_united_states.csv" dataset from your data folder.

Explore the variables using functions from the `{inspectdf}` package, such as `inspect_cat()`, `inspect_num()`, and `show_plot()`.

## TASK 3: CLEAN THE COLUMN NAMES

Some columns, including several comorbidity columns (e.g. `coronary.artery.disease`, `cerebrovascular.disease`), contain dots that make them challenging to work with in R. Use `clean_names()` from the `{janitor}` package to address this issue. Store the output as a data frame called `covid_us_clean`.

## TASK 4: RENAME AND TRANSFORM VARIABLES

Transform the data by doing the following, and store the results as `covid_us_clean2`:

- Rename the `group` column to `status`. Use the `rename()` function to perform this change.
- Change the capitalization of the `sex` values ("male" and "female") to title case using `mutate()` and `str_to_title()`.
- Change the capitalization of the `race` values ("black", "white", "hispanic", etc.) to title case in the same `mutate()` call.

## TASK 5: CREATE A SUBSET

Create a subset of your data by doing the following, and store it as `covid_us_subset`:

- Keep only the following columns using the `select()` function: `id`, `sex`, `age`, `race`, `status`, and `hospital`.
- Use the `filter()` function to keep only rows where `status` is "Expired" AND `race` is NOT "Unknown".

**CHECK**: Your dataset should have 684 rows and 6 columns.

## TASK 6: SUMMARIZE DATA

Using the subset created in Task 5, construct a summary table that displays the number of deaths per race and sex.

**HINT**: Use the `count()` function from `{dplyr}`. You could also do the same thing using a combination of `group_by()` and `summarize()`, but `count()` is the more efficient option.

**CHECK**: Your summary table should have 10 rows and 3 columns. The first few rows of your summary table should look like this:

+---------+---------+---------+
| race    | sex     | n       |
|         |         |         |
| \<chr\> | \<chr\> | \<int\> |
+:========+:========+========:+
| Asian   | Female  | 16      |
+---------+---------+---------+
| Asian   | Male    | 32      |
+---------+---------+---------+
| Black   | Female  | 108     |
+---------+---------+---------+
| Black   | Male    | 126     |
+---------+---------+---------+

## TASK 7: VISUALIZE SUMMARY DATA

Using the summary table you created in the previous step, create a stacked bar plot using `{ggplot2}` to illustrate the number of deaths per race, segmented by sex.

Add a title, subtitle, and caption to your plot that provide context and explain the data being visualized. Customize the theme.

**HINT**: You will need to use the `ggplot()` and `geom_col()` functions to create this plot.

## TASK 8: EXPORT YOUR OUTPUTS

Organize your outputs by creating an "outputs" folder within your project directory.

1.  Export your summary table as a CSV file.

2.  Use `ggsave()` to save your plot.

**HINT**: Save both these files to your "outputs" folder. Make sure to use the `here()` function to specify your file paths.

## TASK 9: ADD INLINE CODE AND COMMENTARY

To finalize your report, include **inline code** in your RMD to quote results from your `race_sex_count` table created in Task 6. There are 3 statistics to be quoted in the text: `max_race_group`, `max_sex_group`, and `max_n_deaths`.

First, complete the code to extract `max_race_group` and `max_n_deaths` from `race_sex_count`.

Then, replace any placeholders such as `"WRITE_YOUR_INLINE_CODE_HERE"` with actual inline code to dynamically display your findings.

Quoting results with inline code can be tricky, so we've completed one answer as an example for you. Feel free to adapt this code for the remaining two answers.

**CHECK**: When you knit your document, the text below Task 9 should read as:

> The demographic group with the highest number of COVID-19 deaths was White Males, with 199 deaths.

## TASK 10: CREATE A DEMOGRAPHIC SUBSET & SUMMARY

Create a summary table that displays the racial breakdown of expired male patients, and render it using `{reactable}` in your knitted document.

For this, use the `covid_us_subset` by doing the following, and store it as `expired_demographics`:

- Use the `filter()` function to ONLY include participants where `sex` is `Male` AND `hospital` is `Maimonides`.
- Construct a summary table that displays the count of these patients by `race` using the `count()` function from `{dplyr}`.
- Use the `reactable()` function from `{reactable}` to render the table.

**CHECK**: Your `expired_demographics` summary table should have 5 rows and 2 columns. The first few rows of your summary table should look like this:

+------------+---------+
| race       | n       |
|            |         |
| \<chr\>    | \<int\> |
+:===========+========:+
| Asian      | 32      |
+------------+---------+
| Black      | 23     |
+------------+---------+
| Hispanic   | 1       |
+------------+---------+

## TASK 11: KNIT YOUR RMARKDOWN DOCUMENT

Finally, knit your RMarkdown document to an HTML file. When you knit your file, please turn OFF code echo on all chunks, so that you have a clean output.

Inspect your final HTML to ensure all looks good before submitting.

# Submit Your Work

To submit your completed assignment, upload YOUR assignment Rmd file to the submission page. Please remember to add your name at the top of the document.

Make sure you can knit your document successfully to HTML before uploading to avoid any submission issues.

Happy coding, and good luck!

# Challenge (Optional)

If you're looking for an additional challenge, try the following:

1.  Add text labels to the bars in your plot, to indicate the exact number of deaths for each segment. You can use the `geom_text()` function to achieve this.

2.  Create an additional plot. For example, you could add a line graph or bar graph to represent a time series of the number of deaths per week. Utilize the `select()`, `filter()`, `mutate()`, and plotting functions from `{ggplot2}` to complete this task.

    **HINT**: The `date_admit` column is stored as text in `dd.mm.yy hh:mm` format. You'll need to parse it with `lubridate::dmy_hm()` before plotting.
